questions.stem: HR wants the accounts in a new SaaS app to be created when people join, updated when they change teams, and switched off when they leave, with nobody touching the app by hand. Which tool fits?
options: SAML, because the signed assertion it sends at sign-in tells the app which accounts to keep or switch off
JIT provisioning, because the app builds each account itself from the details sent at the person's first sign-in
LDAP, because the app can check every person's password against the company's own directory service
SCIM, because the identity provider itself creates, updates and deactivates the accounts in the app for you
questions.explanation: SCIM is the provisioning tool: it creates, updates and deactivates accounts (deactivation sets the account's active field to false). SAML only signs a person in and cannot create or remove the account. JIT provisioning creates an account at first sign-in but, per Microsoft Learn, cannot delete or deactivate it, so leavers would stay. LDAP is a way for an app to check passwords, which is a different job and leaves the app handling the password.

questions.stem: You capture a login in Chrome's Network tab. After the redirect to the sign-in page and back to the app, the earlier requests have vanished and you cannot see what was sent. What do you do?
options: Tick Preserve log before repeating the login, so that the redirects no longer clear the Network list
Switch off the browser's cache so each redirect is stored again as a separate request in the list
Clear the user's cookies first, so that the sign-in does not redirect and the whole login stays on one page
Decode the token offline instead, because the Network tab is not able to record a login that redirects
questions.explanation: Each page load or redirect clears the Network list unless you tick Preserve log (Firefox calls the same setting Persist Logs). That is the capture step of the five-step routine. Cache settings do not control whether the list is cleared. Clearing cookies changes the login you are trying to reproduce, which breaks the first step, and decoding a token is a later step that needs the capture first.

questions.stem: A ticket says the HR app shows 'audience not valid'. Your SAML capture shows Audience https://hr.example.com/saml/v2, while the app's setup lists its entity ID as https://hr.example.com/saml. What do you hand to the identity admin?
options: The capture time: the assertion is valid only between two times and the clocks on the two sides probably disagree
The certificate end date: the app's stored copy of the IdP certificate has probably expired and the signature check on the assertion is failing
Both IDs: the assertion is addressed to an audience that differs from the app's own entity ID, so they must be made identical
The redirect URI: the registered return address probably differs from the one in the request by a trailing slash
questions.explanation: The app accepts an assertion only if its own entity ID is listed as the audience, and the capture shows a different value. Hand over both values, change nothing yourself, and let the admin change one setting and retest. A clock problem would read 'expired' or 'not yet valid', a certificate problem would read 'signature invalid', and a redirect URI problem shows an error page at the IdP, so none of those match this message.

questions.stem: An API answers 401 invalid_token. You decode the token offline: its exp reads 2026-09-21T14:18:20Z and today is 2026-10-06. What does that tell you?
options: The token's scopes are too small, so the caller must ask for broader permissions before retrying the request
The token expired long ago, so the caller needs a fresh one from the identity provider; the API is not at fault
The app's own login to the identity provider failed, so its client ID and secret need checking in the setup
The token was tampered with, because a decoded token whose expiry is wrong has always had its signature altered
questions.explanation: exp is the expiry time, and a 401 invalid_token means the access token is expired, revoked or malformed; here the decoded exp is two weeks old. Too-small scopes produce 403 insufficient_scope instead. A failed login of the app itself is invalid_client at the token endpoint, a different step. Decoding only reads the token and never checks its signature, so an old exp says nothing about tampering.

questions.stem: Your provisioning tool reports 409 Conflict with scimType uniqueness when creating Bob@Example.com. A search in the app finds bob@example.com already there. What is going on?
options: An account with that userName already exists and userName ignores capitals, so link the existing account instead
The app's server has crashed, so the request should simply be sent again after the provider has restarted it
Bob's existing account is switched off with active set to false, and the app blocks any new account for that name
The tool's login to the app has expired, so it should fetch a new bearer token and then repeat the create request
questions.explanation: A 409 on create means the app refused to create a duplicate resource, and userName must be unique and ignores capital letters, so Bob@Example.com collides with bob@example.com. The right move is to find the existing account by username and link it. A crashed server would not answer with a SCIM uniqueness error, and the active field says whether a user can sign in; it is not what triggers this refusal.

questions.stem: At 10:00 HR disables a leaver and the identity provider sets the account's active field to false in the app. At 10:20 the person still has the app open and is still working. Why?
options: The app ignored the deactivation, because a switched-off account is only blocked at the next password change
The app decides what active false means, and many apps leave a session or token already issued working until its exp
The SAML assertion that signed the person in stays valid for ever, so no later change can end the session
The identity provider keeps the account alive for a day after deactivation, so that an HR mistake could be undone first
questions.explanation: Setting active to false is only a request to the app: the app decides what it means, and many apps do not end a session or token that was already issued. A token works until its exp, which is why the architect's question 'what happens to a leaver' also asks about sessions and tokens. Nothing in this lesson says a switched-off account is blocked only at the next password change. Assertions are valid only between two times, not for ever, and nothing says accounts linger for a day, so the check that matters is how long the app's sessions last.
